# Duplication audit (#1053 priority 0, #1054)

**Generated by `tools/duplication_audit.py`; do not edit by hand.**

Both issues open with the same missing item: an audit of duplication across the rules layers. Extracting an engine-independent rules package is not possible while the same rule is implemented several times, because moving one copy leaves the others answering differently.

This is the **static** half of the audit: where the same rule is implemented more than once. It cannot tell you whether those copies *behave* the same, and it must not pretend to — a different body can compute the identical answer. That question is answered by the behavioural probe in `docs/RULES_PARITY_1053.md`, which calls every layer with the same character.

| Finding | Meaning | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| **Byte-identical copy** | same body in several homes | consolidation: debt, not yet a bug |
| **Differing implementation** | same rule, different code | behaviour unknown from source alone — run `tools/rules_parity_probe.py` |

| Measure | Count |
|---|---:|
| Rule names defined in more than one file | **28** |
| …of those, **implemented differently** (behaviour unknown from source) | **26** |
| Redundant copies to remove | **41** |
| Rules implemented in both Python and GDScript | **100** |

## How this was measured

Definitions are collected with `ast` from `src/rules/`, `mud/nopunk_mud/`, `mud/systems/` and
`strategy_game/`, and with a `func` regex from `godot/core/`. Functions are grouped by name; bodies are
fingerprinted with docstrings removed so that a comment change is not mistaken for a behaviour change.
`legacy/` is excluded because it is a frozen historical record that must not be modernised.

A name match is evidence, not proof: two files may legitimately define `chase_modifier_table` in
different layers. The fingerprint is what separates a real duplicate from a coincidence of naming, and
the diverging table is the one to read first.
